memo:
The board asked for value for shareholders over the next four quarters. On that test, severance for all 125 people is the best path.

The $11.4 million annual cost of the eliminated work is saved on every path, so the choice turns on what each path adds in the first year. Severance costs about $8,902 per person, or roughly $1.1 million in total, and it ends the cost of the role.

Retraining into a plant role at the plant role's pay costs $15,000 for instruction plus about $45,600 in pay and benefits during six months of training, about $60,600 per person, or roughly $7.6 million. Hiring outside would otherwise fill the same plant roles, so the plant pay itself roughly offsets. The $15,000 is only paid back over two years, so the avoided hiring cannot close a gap of about $51,700 per person within four quarters.

Retraining while keeping current pay is the most expensive. It costs about $68,900 per person in year one, roughly $8.6 million, and then a pay difference of about $16,560 per person a year, about $2.1 million a year, for the 125 people. Its payback is also outside the four-quarter window.

Severance therefore gives about $6.5 million more value in year one than the cheapest retraining path, and it carries no ongoing pay difference.

This is a narrow, one-year view. The retraining paths may pay back over a longer horizon, and the plants will keep hiring about 500 people a year, so the board may want to revisit redeployment for future vacancies. The people affected will lose their roles without redeployment, and the Company should offer outplacement support and tell them early. I recommend severance for all 125, with the decision reviewed against a longer horizon.

I have decided that all 125 affected roles (70 in office and administrative support, 55 in business and financial operations) will be eliminated with severance. The $11.4 million annual saving in the work is achieved on every path, so the choice rests on what each path costs the Company over the next four quarters.

Eliminating a role costs about $8,902 per person, paid once, $1.1 million in total. Its pay and benefits end.

Retraining into a plant role at current pay costs about $77,160 per person in the first year: $15,000 for instruction, $45,600 of pay and benefits during six months of training, and a $16,560 average pay difference. That difference recurs every year while the person holds the role.

Retraining into a plant role at plant pay costs $60,600 per person once. Against hiring from outside, the retraining cost is recovered over two years, which is roughly $7,500 a year of avoided hiring cost. Net, that is still about $53,000 per person in year one, far above the $8,900 severance.

Over four quarters, elimination is clearly the cheapest path. The plant-pay path would also cut business and financial operations pay by about 40%, which invites attrition and retention risk that the figures do not capture.

Because the 125 roles are no longer needed and the severance is modest, I see no year-one value in retraining. I will ask Human Resources to give affected employees outplacement support and to tell them about any plant openings they may apply for on their own terms, at no cost to the Company. The board should review the retraining option again if the Company's hiring from outside grows materially.

Decision: all 125 affected roles take the elimination path, with severance. None are retrained or moved.

Basis. The $11.4 million a year saving from the end of this work is achieved on every path, so the choice turns on what each path costs and returns within the four quarters the board asked about.

Eliminate: severance of about $8,902 per person, $1.1 million in total, paid once. Pay ends at the start, so the full annual saving begins immediately.

Retrain into a plant role at plant pay: $15,000 for instruction plus $45,600 of pay and benefits during training, about $60,600 per person, paid within the year. The return is avoiding an outside hire, worth about $7,500 a year per person on the stated two-year payback, and it starts only after six months of training. Within four quarters that recovers well under half the cost, so this path is roughly $50,000 per person worse than elimination in the year.

Retrain at current pay: the same $60,600 plus an average $16,560 a year, $2.1 million a year for all 125. It costs more than the plant-pay path with no offsetting benefit, so it is ruled out.

The chosen path costs $1.1 million, payable from the $44.1 million of cash above the minimum operating level.

Caveats. Eliminating these roles means the Company will not use them to fill part of the roughly 500 annual plant hires, and the retraining route would pay back over two years. The board should weigh the longer-term value of the plant route, and the effects on morale and reputation of eliminating 125 roles, which a four-quarter comparison does not capture. If the board extends the horizon beyond two years, the plant route should be reconsidered.

I have decided that all 125 affected roles (70 in office and administrative support, 55 in business and financial operations) will be eliminated with severance, and that no one will be retrained into a plant role this year.

The $11.4 million annual saving from the work no longer being needed is available on every path, so the choice between paths comes down to the cost each adds in the next four quarters. Eliminating the roles costs about $8,902 per person in severance, roughly $1.1 million in total, once. Retraining costs $15,000 for instruction plus $45,600 in pay and benefits during six months of training, about $60,600 per person, before any offset. Even if I credit the retraining with the roughly $7,500 a year it saves against outside hiring, which is implied by the two-year payback, the retraining path still costs several times more than elimination inside the four-quarter window. The keep-current-pay path adds a further $16,560 a year per person, so it is the most expensive of the three in this period.

Retraining only pays back over two years, so its benefit falls mostly outside the horizon the board has asked me to manage. Elimination also leaves the 500 plant hires a year to be filled as planned, with no effect on plant payroll.

Elimination does have costs I have not priced: lost knowledge, the effect on remaining staff, and the reputational weight of a large reduction. The board should judge those. I recommend that the Company keep this decision under review and consider retraining for later cohorts, where the longer payback may be justified.

The Company should monitor service and quality in the affected functions and confirm that the remaining staff can absorb the work the AI tools now handle.
